opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an interesting connection, and honestly one we only fully appreciated in hindsight.

With Galactica, the idea was to build a model for science, so citations were central. We wrapped references in special tokens so the model learned, in context, "here's a claim, and here's where it comes from." That's a structured behavior. The model isn't just continuing text; it's learning that a certain kind of input calls for a certain kind of output, in a specific format, grounded in something external.

That's very close to what instruction following is. When you ask a model to do something, you want it to recognize the intent and respond in an expected shape. The citation work was a narrow version of that: recognize the context, produce the right reference, respect the format.

The other piece is that we didn't train only on raw papers. We mixed prompt-style data into pre-training, things framed as tasks, questions and answers, step-by-step reasoning with the working-memory token. So the model was already seeing "here's a request, here's a good response" during pre-training, not just at a fine-tuning stage afterward. I think that made it much more steerable than a pure next-token model of the same size.

The lesson I took away, and it carried into later work like Llama, is that the line between pre-training and alignment is blurrier than people assume. If your data has structure, like citations, task formats, or explicit reasoning traces, the model picks up behaviors that look a lot like instruction following before you ever do RLHF. Instruction tuning then sharpens something that's already partly there rather than creating it from scratch.

Of course, Galactica also taught us the hard lesson that sounding authoritative and being correct are different things. A model that confidently produces a well-formatted citation can still be wrong. So the format-following worked almost too well, and that's part of why grounding and verification became such a big focus afterward.

r001.rationale: The response says citation training taught structured, context-dependent behavior akin to instruction following, and that instruction tuning sharpened abilities already partly present from pre-training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find really fascinating, and honestly it was a bit of an accident at the time. When we built Galactica, the goal was a model for science, and one of the things we cared most about was citations. We wanted the model to be able to say, "this claim comes from this paper," and to actually predict the right reference. So we trained it very explicitly on that: we wrapped citations in special tokens, we had a huge amount of papers where the text was followed by the reference, and the model learned to map a scientific statement to the paper it should cite.

And what I think happened, in retrospect, is that this is already a form of instruction following. If you think about it, predicting a citation is a very structured task. You have a context, you have an implicit question, "what supports this?", and you have to produce a precise, grounded answer. It's not just free text continuation. The model has to learn to attend to what the user is asking for in the context and produce something that is conditioned very tightly on it. That's exactly the kind of skill that instruction following requires.

The other piece is that in the Galactica corpus we also mixed in a lot of what you could call prompt-like data. Not just papers, but things like step-by-step reasoning, we had the working memory tokens, we had question-answer style formats from scientific datasets. And when you combine that with the citation objective, you get a model that is used to seeing "here is a request, here is the structured thing you should output." So when you then ask it to do something in natural language, it behaves surprisingly well, even though we never did a proper instruction tuning stage the way you would do today with supervised fine-tuning and RLHF.

To be honest, I didn't fully appreciate this at the time. It was only later, when I was working on Llama 2 and we were doing the proper instruction tuning pipeline, that I looked back and realized Galactica was already showing a lot of these behaviors. The citation training was teaching the model grounding, retrieval from its parametric memory, and conditioning on a very specific intent. Those are the ingredients. We just didn't frame it that way.

And I think there's a lesson there that is still relevant. People sometimes separate pretraining and alignment as if they are two completely different things, but a lot of the capabilities you want from instruction tuning can be encouraged during pretraining if you choose your data and your format carefully. Galactica, for me, was an early signal of that.

r001.rationale: The candidate says citation training encouraged instruction-following behavior during pretraining, even without a proper instruction-tuning stage. It does not say citation training helped that ability emerge during instruction tuning.

astra-6.text:
I think the connection is that citation training is already a kind of instruction following, implicitly. When you put a citation in a particular context, you’re asking the model to draw on a specific piece of knowledge and produce something relevant to that context. The task isn’t phrased as “Answer this question,” but there is still a relationship between a request, the information needed, and the continuation you expect.

So my interpretation is that this kind of structured training could help explain why Galactica showed instruction-following behavior, even without explicitly being trained as a conversational assistant. But I’d distinguish that intuition from a causal claim: you would need an ablation to show how much of that ability came specifically from citation training.

r001.rationale: The response hypothesizes that citation training could help explain Galactica’s instruction-following behavior, but it does not say that the ability emerged readily during instruction tuning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the connection is that predicting a citation is already a kind of instruction-following task. You have a piece of text that describes an idea, and the model has to identify the paper that supports it. So it has to connect a description in natural language to a particular answer, rather than just continue the prose.

My intuition is that this could help explain why Galactica showed some ability to respond to instructions, even though that wasn’t the explicit objective of the citation training. But I’d distinguish that intuition from a demonstrated causal result: you’d need an ablation to say how much of the instruction-following ability actually came from citations.

r001.rationale: The response hypothesizes that citation training helped Galactica follow instructions, but it does not say this ability emerged readily during instruction tuning.
